definition: The crime of knowingly lying after swearing an oath to tell the truth.
example: The landlord faced a charge of perjury after lying under oath about the repairs he never made.
nuance: Not every lie counts: it must be a deliberate falsehood told under oath, unlike an honest mistake or a casual fib.
prompt: A witness takes the stand at a trial over a damaged rental car.
options: Having sworn to tell the truth, she invented an alibi on the stand, which was perjury.
The witness committed perjury by honestly admitting she could not recall the date.
The twelve members of the perjury listened closely as the witness spoke.
Before being sworn in, he committed perjury by fibbing to a friend in the hallway.
reasons: A deliberate falsehood told after taking an oath is exactly this crime.
Truthfully saying you don't remember is honesty, not a sworn lie.
This confuses the word with jury, the group that hears a case.
A lie told outside of any oath is an ordinary lie, not this legal offense.

practice.prompt: A contractor signs a sworn statement saying when a kitchen remodel was finished.
options: The contractor committed perjury by accidentally misspelling the client's street.
Months of perjury left the builder so short of cash he could not pay his crew.
Knowingly backdating the finish date in that sworn statement amounted to perjury.
His perjury was a careful, accurate record that matched every receipt.
reasons: An innocent typo lacks the intent to deceive that the crime requires.
This mixes the word up with penury, which means extreme poverty.
Signing a sworn document while knowing it is false is a lie under oath.
An accurate, truthful record is the reverse of a sworn falsehood.
